To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) GPUs can be used for real-time applications in the context of high energy physics experiments, (2) the use of GPUs can reduce the latency and increase the throughput of the trigger systems, and (3) GPUs can be exploited to reduce the complexity of the trigger systems and, in particular, of the high level trigger.
the use of GPUs in online computing is possible, and that it is a promising approach for the development of trigger-less systems.

1) GPUs are mature for use in online applications; 2) GPUs can be successfully exploited for the implementation of synchronous low level triggers with fixed latency, as demonstrated by the first field test within NA62; 3) GPUs can be exploited in online high level triggers, as demonstrated by a case study on the ATLAS experiment at LHC.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the use of GPUs for online applications.
the use of GPUs for online applications in high energy particle physics, in the fields of data acquisition and trigger.

the development of new techniques and algorithms for the use of GPU computing in online trigger systems for high energy physics, with the ultimate goal of developing a trigger system based on a purely software approach, i.e. trigger-less.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the GPU technology can provide a powerful tool for the online trigger and data acquisition system in the next generation of high energy physics experiments.
the use of GPUs in online applications for high energy experiments, and in particular in triggering systems, is still in its infancy.
GPUs can be successfully employed for the implementation of online trigger systems.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the use of GPU-based parallel computing in high energy physics is still at its very beginning, but it has the potential of being a very powerful and flexible tool for online applications.
we are able to use a GPU to perform the same task as a CPU, but at least 10 times faster, and with a power consumption that is 10 to 100 times smaller.

the GPU technology can be used in both early trigger stages and high level trigger systems, and that GPUs are a viable alternative to traditional FPGAs for implementing trigger functions in a trigger-less scenario.
The main takeaway from our work is that

GPU technology can be successfully applied to online triggering applications, both in low and high level trigger stages, and that it can represent a very interesting alternative to the use of general-purpose multicore CPU systems.
the use of GPUs in online computing is feasible and can lead to a substantial improvement of the performance of trigger and data acquisition systems.

GPUs can be used for online parallel computing in real-time applications, and can be used for both low level and high level triggers, with a significant reduction in the overall latency and in the cost of the computing farm.
